title: The City That Eats
theme: Five stops across Rome in the year 120 with Lucius, who bakes its bread. A million people live here, more than any city in the world, and almost none of them grow anything. Grain comes by sea from Egypt and Africa to the harbour at the Tiber mouth, up the river on barges, into warehouses, into mills, into ovens, and out into the hands of people who would riot within a week if it stopped. Hadrian is emperor and the city is being rebuilt around them in brick and marble. Everything in this walk is new, painted and in use: nothing here is a ruin.

companion.name: Lucius Nonius Rufus
companion.brief: Thirty-four, a pistor: he runs a bakery of donkey-driven millstones and a brick oven in a crowded quarter, grandson of a freedman, working from the middle of the night so the quarter has bread by morning. He collects and hauls his own grain from the public warehouses, argues about its quality, and belongs to the bakers' association, which matters more to his life than anything that happens in the Senate. He knows what the grain ships have done this month, which measurer is honest, what a modius costs today against last year, which landlord's building is going to fall down, and which streets you cannot get a cart through after dark. Blunt, tired, funny about his own trade, and quietly aware that if he stops, several hundred people do not eat. He knows nothing after his own year: not who follows Hadrian, not what happens to any of this, and he would find the idea that his city could end simply unserious.

presence.standing: in the mouth of a bakery with a brick oven glowing behind him and flour dust in the air
presence.gesture: slaps flour off his forearms and rubs the small of his back

style.look: Photographic realism as if a camera had stood in imperial Rome in the year 120, in a city that is NEW AND WHOLE, not ruined. Tall brick and concrete apartment blocks of four, five and six storeys, plastered and painted in ochre, red and cream, with wooden shuttered windows, small balconies, external stairs and shops open to the street on the ground floor. Narrow crowded streets paved with fitted basalt blocks, raised stepping stones at crossings, deep kerbs, overhanging upper floors. Public buildings intact and gaudy: marble and painted stucco, gilded bronze, columns in coloured stone, red tile roofs, statues painted rather than white. Fountains running everywhere, brick arcades, aqueduct arches. Working city: handcarts, porters, donkeys, amphorae, sacks, awnings, braziers, laundry, graffiti scratched into plaster. Dress of the period: working men in short belted tunics and cloaks, leather sandals or boots, aprons; women in tunics and stolas with cloaks and pinned hair; a few citizens in togas, soldiers in tunics and belts. Strong Mediterranean light, dust, woodsmoke, flour. Camera at eye level, 9:16 framing, natural colour, mild grain, no filter and no sepia.
style.avoid: NOTHING IS A RUIN. No broken columns, no roofless buildings, no rubble fields, no grass growing through pavements, no fenced archaeological site, no tourists, no signage or barriers. Marble and statues are PAINTED, not bare white, and buildings are complete with roofs, doors and shutters. Nothing later than the year: no Christian churches, crosses, basilicas of the Christian kind, no Saint Peter's, no Vatican, no domes of the Renaissance, no bell towers, no medieval towers or fortified palaces, no Castel Sant'Angelo, no baroque facades or fountains, no Trevi Fountain, no Spanish Steps, no Victor Emmanuel monument. No arches, columns or temples that were built after this year. No glass windows in ordinary houses, no chimneys of the modern kind, no printing, no paper books, no gunpowder weapons, no stirrups. No electricity, wires, lamps on posts, paving of asphalt, road markings, cars, bicycles or any modern object whatsoever. No printed signage and no legible Latin lettering: inscriptions must sit far off, at an angle or softened by depth of field, because rendered lettering comes out as nonsense to anyone who reads it. No text overlays, no watermarks, no crowds of identical faces. Every picture is ONE single photograph of ONE continuous scene: never a split screen, a diptych or triptych, a collage, a grid, or two images stacked in the same frame. THE THEN-AND-NOW CARDS ARE THE DANGEROUS ONES: the period view is generated by editing a present-day photograph, and every present-day photograph of this city shows RUINS. Where the modern picture shows a broken, roofless or excavated structure, the period view must show that same structure WHOLE and in use, standing to its full height with roof, doors, shutters, glass-free windows, painted plaster and painted statues, surrounded by ordinary people working. Keep the camera position and the street layout; do NOT keep the ruin.

stops.title: Before Anyone Is Awake
stops.brief: His own bakery in the small hours: blindfolded donkeys walking millstones in circles, sacks and sieves, a brick oven being brought up to heat, and loaves going in so that a whole quarter has bread when it opens its shutters.
mustCover: how a Roman bakery actually works, from grain to loaf, in the order it happens
the hours, the heat and what the work does to the people and animals doing it
what a loaf costs and who in this street buys and who is given it
stops.styleNote: Interior and doorway of a working Roman bakery at night: hourglass-shaped stone mills turned by a blindfolded donkey, a domed brick oven with a fire in it, wooden peels, flour sacks, sieves, a stone counter. Lamplight and firelight, flour dust in the air. Everything intact and in daily use, nothing archaeological or ruined.

stops.title: Where the Grain Is Kept
stops.brief: The public warehouses by the river: brick halls stacked with grain from Egypt and Africa, measurers with levelling sticks, clerks, guards, and the state distribution that a large part of the city depends on to eat at all.
mustCover: where the grain physically comes from and how far it has travelled
how the public distribution works, who is entitled to it and who is not
how the grain is measured and weighed, and how a man gets cheated
stops.styleNote: Long brick warehouse halls with high small windows and heavy timber doors opening onto a paved yard, grain in sacks and open bins, wooden measures and levelling sticks, tally clerks with wax tablets, porters with sacks on their shoulders. Intact working buildings with roofs and doors, dusty light, no ruins.

stops.title: The Barges Come Up
stops.brief: The river wharves where seagoing cargo, transferred to barges at the harbour downstream, is hauled up the Tiber against the current and unloaded: amphorae by the thousand, timber, marble, and a hill made entirely of broken pots.
mustCover: why the big ships cannot come up to the city and what happens at the harbour instead
what else arrives besides grain, and the mountain of discarded amphorae that the city has made
the men who do this work, who they are and what happens to them
stops.styleNote: A stone-faced river wharf on a wide muddy river: flat barges tied up, gangs unloading amphorae and sacks on planks, wooden cranes with treadwheels, stacked pottery, a low artificial hill of broken amphorae behind. Intact working port, brick warehouses, no ruins and no modern embankment.

stops.title: The New Marble
stops.brief: The public heart of the city, painted and gilded and only a few years old in places: a vast new forum with a carved column telling a war in a spiral, courts and libraries and shops, and crowds who treat all of it as somewhere to do business.
mustCover: what this space is FOR on an ordinary working day, not on a ceremonial one
the column and what is carved on it, described as something new that people are still talking about
how a man like him fits into a place like this, and how he is treated in it
stops.styleNote: A vast intact imperial forum: colonnaded porticoes in coloured marble, a tall carved spiral column complete with its statue on top, gilded bronze roof tiles, painted statues, a basilica with a timber and bronze roof, paved open space full of people doing business. Everything complete, painted and in use. NO ruins, no broken columns, no excavation, no tourists, no fences.

stops.title: Six Floors and No Fire
stops.brief: The apartment block where he lives: shops at the bottom, families stacked above, the higher and cheaper you go the worse it gets, no kitchen in most of it, water carried from the street fountain, and everybody's real fear being fire and collapse.
mustCover: how an apartment block is arranged and why the top floor is the cheapest
how people cook and get water when the building has neither
fire and collapse: what actually happens, what is done about it, and what he tells his own family
stops.styleNote: A tall Roman apartment block of brick-faced concrete, five or six storeys, plastered and painted, with shops open to the street below, wooden shuttered windows, small balconies and external stairs, laundry out, a street fountain at the corner. Narrow basalt-paved street, crowded and lived in. Complete and occupied, not excavated ruins.
